qs.q: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic GERD and cigarette smoking presents with progressive dyspnea and a dry cough. Histopathology or biopsy is considered unnecessary under specific clinical circumstances. When should a lung biopsy be avoided in suspected IPF?
o: If clinical evidence is typical and HRCT findings are clear
If the patient has concurrent systemic hypertension and proteinuria
If pulmonary function tests show a preserved FEV1/FVC ratio
If the patient is older than sixty years of age overall
qs.e: A surgical lung biopsy should not be performed if the clinical evidence is typical and HRCT findings of usual interstitial pneumonia are clear. Biopsies carry procedural risks that are unnecessary when imaging and clinical features are diagnostic.

qs.q: A lung biopsy shows cells growing in a monolayer along alveolar septa without invasion (2.8 cm). What is the diagnosis?
o: Lepidic‑predominant adenocarcinoma.
Minimally invasive adenocarcinoma.
Adenocarcinoma in situ with lepidic growth.
Squamous cell carcinoma.
qs.e: AIS (formerly BAC) is defined by growth along pre-existing alveolar structures (lepidic growth) without any stromal or vascular invasion.

qs.q: A 35-year-old presents with hemoptysis, anemia, diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Lung biopsy shows linear IgG deposition. The target antigen is
o: Neutrophil proteinase-3
Double-stranded DNA
α3 chain of collagen IV
Myeloperoxidase antigen
qs.e: Goodpasture syndrome is caused by antibodies targeting the noncollagenous domain of the α3 chain of collagen IV, affecting both pulmonary and glomerular basement membranes.

qs.q: A 50-year-old male develops progressive dyspnea over 2 years. Lung biopsy shows honeycomb fibrosis, fibroblastic foci, and temporal heterogeneity. Mean survival from diagnosis is approximately
o: Mean survival of approximately 8 to 10 years with treatment
Mean survival of approximately 5 to 7 years with steroids
Mean survival of approximately 1 to 2 years without transplant
Mean survival of approximately 3 years or less from diagnosis
qs.e: IPF has a mean survival of 3 years or less from diagnosis, with relentless progression despite medical therapy. Lung transplantation is the only definitive treatment.

qs.q: A young man uses intravenous drugs and develops pulmonary hypertension. Lung biopsy shows granulomas with birefringent crystals under polarized light. The likely substance is
o: Magnesium trisilicate (talc) from IV drug mixture
Asbestos fibers from environmental exposure
Silica particles from contaminated needles
Coal dust from occupational inhalation
qs.e: IV drug abuse introduces magnesium trisilicate (talc) as a filler in drug mixtures into the pulmonary microvasculature. Talc elicits a granulomatous response; vascular involvement leads to pulmonary hypertension. Talc crystals are visible by polarized light.

qs.q: Which of the following differentiates NSIP from IPF on lung biopsy?
o: Presence of fibroblastic foci and honeycombing in NSIP
Noncaseating granulomas present only in NSIP
Lower lobe predominance only seen in NSIP
Absence of temporal heterogeneity in NSIP
qs.e: NSIP lacks the temporal heterogeneity of UIP/IPF. In NSIP, fibrosis is uniform (all the same age). Fibroblastic foci and honeycombing are typically absent in NSIP but present in IPF.

qs.q: When a UIP pattern is found on lung biopsy, which of the following must be excluded before diagnosing IPF?
o: Sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia and NSIP
Silicosis and coal worker pneumoconiosis
Collagen vascular diseases and asbestosis
qs.e: UIP pattern can be seen in asbestosis, collagen vascular diseases, drug reactions, and other conditions. These known causes must be excluded before the diagnosis of IPF (idiopathic) can be made.

qs.q: A lung biopsy shows tumour cells growing in a monolayer along alveolar septa without stromal invasion, desmoplasia, or architectural destruction. The lesion measures 2.8 cm. What is the diagnosis?
o: Minimally invasive adenocarcinoma with an invasive component under 5 mm
Adenocarcinoma in situ showing lepidic growth under 3 cm without invasion
Atypical adenomatous hyperplasia representing a well-demarcated focus
Invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma featuring pneumonia-like consolidation
qs.e: AIS is defined by lepidic growth ≤3 cm along pre-existing alveolar septa with absolutely no stromal invasion, desmoplasia, or alveolar architectural destruction.

es.q: A pathologist is reviewing a lung biopsy from a patient with a long history of heavy smoking and chronic cough. Upon microscopic examination, the pathologist measures the Reid Index. a) What specific anatomical feature does the Reid Index quantify? b) What value of the Reid Index is considered indic
es.m: a) The Reid Index measures submucosal gland hypertrophy in the bronchial wall. b) A Reid Index greater than 0.4 indicates significant enlargement, characteristic of chronic bronchitis.

es.q: A lung biopsy from a patient with Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) is submitted for microscopic evaluation. What is the hallmark microscopic finding characteristic of the acute phase of Diffuse Alveolar Damage (DAD)?
es.m: The hallmark microscopic finding characteristic of the acute phase of Diffuse Alveolar Damage (DAD), which is the histologic manifestation of ARDS, is the presence of hyaline membranes lining the alveolar spaces.

es.q: A lung biopsy from a patient with progressive dyspnea reveals patchy fibrosis with temporal heterogeneity, a histologic pattern required for the diagnosis of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF). What is the name of this specific histologic pattern, and what is the typical prognosis for IPF?
es.m: The histologic pattern required for the diagnosis of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP) (3 marks). The mean survival for IPF is typically 3 years or less (2 marks).

es.q: A patient presents with acute onset severe dyspnea, cyanosis, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates refractory to oxygen. A lung biopsy reveals diffuse alveolar damage (DAD). What is the hallmark microscopic finding in DAD, and what severe acute lung injury condition does it characterize?
es.m: The hallmark microscopic finding in Diffuse Alveolar Damage (DAD) is the presence of hyaline membranes. DAD is characteristic of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS).

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Lung biopsy is a key diagnostic tool for interstitial lung disease, infections, and malignancy when imaging is inconclusive. In resource‑limited hospitals, clinical judgment and simple tests guide the choice of biopsy method.

sections.p: A lung biopsy obtains lung tissue for histopathology. It is indicated when imaging, bronchoalveolar lavage, and non‑invasive tests fail to establish a diagnosis.

t.b: Does the CT show a pattern that is diagnostic? If not, biopsy is needed.
Lymphocytosis suggests sarcoidosis or hypersensitivity pneumonitis; neutrophilia points to infection.
Rule out TB or bacterial pneumonia before biopsy.

sections.p: Staging is disease‑specific: for sarcoidosis (Stage I–IV), for interstitial lung disease (ILD) using GAP score, and for malignancy using TNM.

In East Africa, the leading causes of unexplained lung infiltrates are tuberculosis, fungal infections, and parasitic infestations. Non‑infectious causes include sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and malignancy.
Patients often have chronic cough, dyspnoea, weight loss, and night sweats. Physical exam may reveal crackles, clubbing, or pleural rub.
Use the simplest tests first; if unavailable, rely on clinical features and basic imaging.

t.b: Shows infiltrates, nodules, or masses; guides biopsy site.
Positive suggests TB exposure; negative does not exclude active disease.
Leukocytosis with neutrophils indicates bacterial infection; eosinophilia suggests parasitic or allergic disease.
Elevated in infection or inflammation; normal in early sarcoidosis.
Restrictive pattern supports interstitial disease; obstructive suggests COPD.
Obtains fluid for cytology, cultures, and cell counts.

sections.p: Complications include pneumothorax, bleeding, infection, and air leak. Red flags are haemoptysis, sudden drop in oxygen saturation, or hemodynamic instability.
Treat the underlying cause first: anti‑TB therapy, antifungals, or chemotherapy. Supportive care includes oxygen, bronchodilators, and corticosteroids for inflammatory conditions.

Itraconazole for histoplasmosis; avoid in hepatic failure.

sections.p: Regular clinical review, repeat imaging, and monitoring of treatment response. Prevention focuses on TB control, safe handling of animal products, and avoidance of occupational dust.
Pulmonary TB, pneumonia, and lung cancer can mimic interstitial lung disease on imaging.
BAL lymphocytosis can be normal in early sarcoidosis; sputum AFB may be negative in TB due to paucibacillary disease.

faq.q: When is a transbronchial biopsy preferred over VATS?
faq.a: When the lesion is peripheral and accessible via bronchoscope, and the patient cannot tolerate surgery.

faq.q: Can a lung biopsy be done in a patient with HIV?
faq.a: Yes, but ensure CD4 >200 and treat opportunistic infections first.

faq.q: What is the safest needle size for a percutaneous lung biopsy?
faq.a: A 16‑18 gauge core needle balances tissue yield and bleeding risk.

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer presents with chronic cough and dyspnoea; HRCT shows diffuse ground‑glass opacities. What is the next best diagnostic step? — BAL with lymphocyte count; if inconclusive, transbronchial biopsy.
A patient with suspected TB has a negative sputum AFB but a positive Mantoux. What should you do next? — Perform a chest X‑ray and consider a lung biopsy if imaging is non‑diagnostic.
Why are corticosteroids avoided in a patient with active pulmonary TB? — They suppress immunity and worsen infection.
What complication is most common after a transbronchial lung biopsy? — Pneumothorax.

In a low‑resource setting, a patient has a pleural effusion and a normal chest X‑ray. What is the likely diagnosis and next step? — Empyema; perform thoracentesis and send fluid for Gram stain and culture.
A patient with suspected hypersensitivity pneumonitis has a BAL lymphocytosis of 45%. What does this indicate? — Supports the diagnosis; proceed to biopsy if clinical picture is unclear.
What is the main reason for choosing VATS over open lung biopsy? — Less morbidity, quicker recovery, and adequate tissue for diagnosis.
